title: Linux Permissions: A Field Handbook
summary: A complete working guide to the Linux permission model — from the rwx bits and octal notation through chmod, chown, umask, setuid/setgid, the sticky bit, and POSIX ACLs. Covers the kernel-side checks, the practical commands, the classic mistakes, and the security trade-offs of each mechanism.

chapters.title: Why Permissions Exist: The Unix Security Model
points: Linux is multi-user by design: every process runs on behalf of a user identity, and every file belongs to one — permissions are the bridge between them
Every user has a numeric UID; every group has a numeric GID. Names in /etc/passwd and /etc/group are just labels — the kernel only ever compares numbers
UID 0 is root: the kernel skips almost all permission checks for it (governed by capabilities like CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE, not by the rwx bits)
A process carries an identity triple: real UID (who launched it), effective UID (who it acts as for permission checks), saved UID (what it may switch back to)
Every file's inode stores exactly three things for access control: owner UID, group GID, and a 16-bit mode field
The mode field = 4 special bits (setuid, setgid, sticky) + 9 permission bits (3 classes × rwx)
DAC vs MAC: standard Linux permissions are Discretionary Access Control — the owner decides. SELinux/AppArmor add Mandatory Access Control on top, and MAC can deny what DAC allows
Permission checks happen at open() time, not at read() time — a file descriptor opened before a chmod keeps working afterward
`ls -l` decodes the inode: `-rw-r--r-- 1 alice devs 4096 Jan 3 file.txt` = type, 9 bits, link count, owner, group, size
The first character is file type, not a permission: `-` regular, `d` directory, `l` symlink, `c` char device, `b` block device, `s` socket, `p` FIFO
Gotcha: `ls -l` shows the symlink's own mode (`lrwxrwxrwx`) — symlink permissions are meaningless; the target's mode is what governs access

chapters.title: The Nine Bits: r, w, x on Files
points: Three classes, checked in strict order: user (owner) → group → other. First matching class wins and the rest are never consulted
Critical consequence: if you are the owner, group and other bits are ignored for you — `chmod 077 file` locks the owner OUT while letting everyone else in
r (read, value 4) on a file: permits reading contents — open() for reading, cat, cp source
w (write, value 2) on a file: permits modifying contents — truncate, append, overwrite. It does NOT permit deleting or renaming the file
x (execute, value 1) on a file: permits the kernel to exec() it — required for both binaries and scripts
Scripts need BOTH x on the script and r on the script: the interpreter must read the text. Compiled binaries need only x
`./script.sh` without x gives `Permission denied`; `bash script.sh` bypasses it because bash only reads the file — a common trap when tightening permissions
Group membership: a process matches the group class if the file's GID is in its primary OR any supplementary group. `id` shows all of them
Supplementary groups are snapshotted at login — adding a user to a group requires a new session (or `newgrp`) to take effect
The symbolic display order is always fixed: `rwxrwxrwx` = user rwx, group rwx, other rwx; `-` means the bit is off
Example decode: `-rwxr-x---` = owner may read/write/execute, group may read/execute, other has nothing

chapters.title: Directories Are Different: The x Bit Is Search
points: A directory is a table mapping names → inode numbers. rwx bits apply to that table, not to the file contents inside
r on a directory = list the names inside (`ls`). Without it, `ls dir` fails but a known path inside may still work
x on a directory = traverse/search — resolve a name inside it to reach an inode. This is the single most important directory bit
w on a directory = modify the table: create, delete, and rename entries. Deleting a file needs w+x on the PARENT, not w on the file
Consequence: you can delete a file you cannot read, and cannot delete a file you own if the parent directory is not writable by you
r without x (`chmod 400 dir`): `ls dir` lists names but every stat fails — output is names with `?????????` for all metadata
x without r (`chmod 100 dir`): a "dark" directory — you cannot list contents, but `cat dir/secret.txt` works if you know the exact name. Classic obscurity pattern for /home layouts
Traversal requires x on EVERY component of the path: reaching /a/b/c.txt needs x on /, /a, and /a/b
This is why `chmod 700 ~` can break a web server: the daemon can no longer traverse into ~/public_html
Directories almost always want r and x paired — 755 or 750. A directory with r but no x is nearly useless

`chmod -R 644 dir` is the classic catastrophe: it strips x from directories, making the tree untraversable. Use `chmod -R a+rX` — capital X sets x only on directories and on files that already have some x bit

chapters.title: Octal Notation: Reading Permissions as Numbers
points: Each rwx triad is a 3-bit binary number: r=4, w=2, x=1. Sum them for a digit 0–7
Full mapping table: 0=---, 1=--x, 2=-w-, 3=-wx, 4=r--, 5=r-x, 6=rw-, 7=rwx
Three digits = user, group, other. `750` = rwx / r-x / ---
A leading fourth digit is the special bits: setuid=4, setgid=2, sticky=1. `4755` = setuid + rwxr-xr-x
When omitted, the leading digit is treated as 0 — and an explicit `chmod 0755` CLEARS any special bits that were set
Common file modes to memorize: 644 (rw-r--r--, normal file), 600 (private file), 664 (group-writable file), 400 (read-only, immutable-ish)
Common directory modes: 755 (standard), 750 (group-private), 700 (fully private), 1777 (world-writable with sticky, i.e. /tmp)
Common script/binary modes: 755 (executable by all), 700 (private script), 4755 (setuid binary — audit these)
Conversion drill: rw-r----- → user 4+2=6, group 4, other 0 → 640
Reverse drill: 2775 → sticky? no; setgid yes; rwx / rwx / r-x — the standard shared project directory
`stat -c '%a %A %U %G' file` prints octal, symbolic, owner, and group together — the fastest way to verify a mode

chapters.title: chmod: Changing Modes
points: Two syntaxes: absolute octal (`chmod 644 f`) which sets all bits at once, and symbolic (`chmod u+x f`) which edits bits relative to current state
Symbolic grammar: [who][op][perm] — who ∈ u,g,o,a; op ∈ +,-,=; perm ∈ r,w,x,X,s,t and the copy sources u,g,o
`+` adds bits, `-` removes bits, `=` sets exactly (clearing unlisted bits in that class): `chmod g=r f` gives group read only
Omitting `who` means "all" but masked by the umask: `chmod +w f` respects umask, while `chmod a+w f` does not — a real and surprising difference
Comma-separated clauses apply in order: `chmod u=rwx,g=rx,o= dir` is equivalent to 750
Copy syntax: `chmod g=u file` makes group permissions identical to user permissions
`X` (capital) = conditional execute — apply x only if the target is a directory or already has x for someone. The safe recursion tool
`chmod -R u+rwX,go+rX,go-w dir` is the canonical "make this tree readable and traversable, writable only by me" recipe
`--reference=FILE` copies another file's mode: `chmod --reference=good.conf new.conf`
Only the file's owner or root may chmod — being in the file's group is not enough, and even a writable file cannot be chmod'ed by a non-owner
chmod does not follow symlinks (the mode of a symlink is not settable on Linux); it acts on the target when the path resolves through one
Practical audit: `find /usr/local -perm -o+w -type f` finds world-writable files; `find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null` finds every setuid binary

chapters.title: chown and chgrp: Changing Ownership
points: `chown user file` sets owner; `chown user:group file` sets both; `chown :group file` sets group only; `chgrp group file` is the dedicated group form
Only root may give a file away to another user — otherwise users could dodge disk quotas or plant files as someone else
A non-root owner may change the file's group, but only to a group they belong to
Security rule: chown by a non-root user clears the setuid and setgid bits, preventing a "hand someone a setuid shell" attack. The kernel does this silently
`chown -R` recurses; `chown -h` acts on a symlink itself rather than its target
`chown -R user:group /` style typos are catastrophic and hard to undo — verify the path, and prefer `--from=olduser:oldgroup` to scope the change
`chown --reference=template file` copies ownership from another file
Numeric IDs work directly (`chown 1000:1000 file`) and are what you need when the name is not in /etc/passwd — common in containers and on mounted foreign filesystems
UID mismatch across systems: a tarball or NFS mount preserves numbers, so UID 1000 on one host may be a different person on another. Use `tar --numeric-owner` deliberately
`cp` creates a new file owned by the copier; `mv` within a filesystem preserves owner and inode. `cp -p`/`cp -a` preserve mode, timestamps, and (as root) ownership
Diagnostic pattern: files owned by a service user but created by a deploy running as root are the most common cause of "permission denied" in production

chapters.title: umask: The Default-Permission Filter
points: umask is a per-process mask of bits to REMOVE from the permissions a program requests at creation time
The formula is a bit-clear, not a subtraction: final = requested AND NOT umask. Thinking of it as 666 − umask happens to work for common values but breaks for odd ones
Programs request base modes: 0666 for regular files, 0777 for directories. The kernel never sets x on a new regular file — that is why a 022 umask yields 644 for files and 755 for directories
umask 022 (default on most distros): group and other lose w. Files 644, directories 755
umask 002 (common in shared-group setups): only other loses w. Files 664, directories 775 — pairs with setgid directories
umask 077 (hardened): group and other lose everything. Files 600, directories 700
`umask` with no arguments prints the octal mask; `umask -S` prints symbolic form; `umask 027` sets it for the current shell and its children only
umask is inherited by child processes and is not persistent — set it in /etc/profile, ~/.bashrc, a systemd unit's `UMask=`, or /etc/login.defs UMASK
umask cannot add permission, only remove it. If a program requests 0600, a umask of 000 will not make the file group-readable
Trap: umask applies at creation only. Existing files are untouched, so changing umask never fixes an already-wrong tree — that needs chmod
Trap: `install`, `cp -p`, `tar -x` (as root), and `git checkout` can bypass or partially bypass umask because they set modes explicitly
Worked example: umask 027, `touch f` → 640; `mkdir d` → 750; a program calling open(..., 0666) still yields 640

chapters.title: setuid and setgid: Borrowed Privilege
points: setuid (mode bit 4000) on an executable makes the process's effective UID become the FILE OWNER's UID at exec time instead of the caller's
setgid (mode bit 2000) on an executable does the same for the effective GID using the file's group
Shows in `ls -l` as `s` in place of x: `-rwsr-xr-x`. A capital `S` means the bit is set but x is NOT — almost always a mistake
Canonical example: /usr/bin/passwd is `-rwsr-xr-x root root` so an ordinary user can edit /etc/shadow (mode 000, root-owned) through a controlled program
Other classic setuid binaries: sudo, su, mount, ping (increasingly replaced by file capabilities like cap_net_raw)

setuid is ignored on shell scripts by every modern Linux kernel — the interpreter/script race (the #! lookup and the exec are not atomic) made it unfixable. Use sudo rules or a small compiled wrapper instead
setuid is ignored on filesystems mounted `nosuid` — the standard hardening for /tmp, /home, and removable media

Writing a setuid program is security-critical: sanitize the environment (PATH, LD_PRELOAD, IFS), drop privileges as early as possible with setresuid(), and validate every path against symlink and TOCTOU races
The saved UID lets a program temporarily drop to the real UID and regain privilege; permanently dropping requires setresuid(uid,uid,uid) — forgetting the saved UID is a classic exploitable bug

setgid on a DIRECTORY means something entirely different: new files and subdirectories inherit the directory's GID rather than the creator's primary group, and subdirectories inherit the setgid bit itself
That directory behaviour is the standard shared-project pattern: `chgrp devs /srv/proj && chmod 2775 /srv/proj`, plus umask 002 so group-write survives
Audit regularly: `find / -xdev \( -perm -4000 -o -perm -2000 \) -type f -exec ls -l {} +` — an unexpected setuid binary is a strong compromise signal

chapters.title: The Sticky Bit: Shared Directories Without Chaos
points: Sticky bit = mode 1000, shown as `t` in the other-execute position: `drwxrwxrwt`. A capital `T` means sticky without x
On a directory it restricts deletion and renaming: only the file's owner, the directory's owner, or root may remove an entry — even though everyone has w on the directory
Without it, world-writable /tmp would let any user delete or replace any other user's temp files
Canonical modes: /tmp and /var/tmp are 1777; /dev/shm is 1777
Set with `chmod +t dir` or `chmod 1777 dir`; clear with `chmod -t dir`
The historical meaning on executables (keep the text segment in swap) is obsolete and ignored by Linux — the bit only matters on directories now
Sticky does not stop overwriting an existing file's CONTENTS if that file is itself writable — it only guards the directory entry
The remaining /tmp attack surface is symlink and hardlink races, mitigated by the kernel's fs.protected_symlinks and fs.protected_hardlinks sysctls (on by default)
Correct practice for temp files: use mkstemp(3) or `mktemp` rather than a predictable name, so an attacker cannot pre-create the path
Audit for world-writable directories missing the bit: `find / -xdev -type d -perm -0002 ! -perm -1000`

chapters.title: POSIX ACLs: Beyond Owner/Group/Other
points: The three-class model cannot express "alice and bob may write, carol may only read" without inventing a group. ACLs add per-user and per-group entries
Requires filesystem support and the `acl` mount option (default on modern ext4/xfs/btrfs). A `+` after the mode in `ls -l` signals an ACL is present
`getfacl file` prints the entries; `setfacl -m u:alice:rw file` adds one; `setfacl -x u:alice file` removes it; `setfacl -b file` strips all extended entries
Entry types: user::, user:name:, group::, group:name:, mask::, other::
The mask is the ceiling: the effective permission of every named user, named group, and group:: entry is its own bits ANDed with the mask. getfacl prints `#effective:` when the mask clips an entry
chmod's group digit rewrites the MASK, not group::, on an ACL file — so `chmod 750` can silently disable ACL entries you thought were active. The single biggest ACL gotcha
Default ACLs on a directory are inheritance templates: `setfacl -d -m g:devs:rwx dir` makes every new child inherit that entry. They affect nothing about the directory's own access
Default ACLs also override umask for files created inside — the inherited entries win
Recursive apply: `setfacl -R -m u:deploy:rX /srv/app`; combine with `-d` in a second pass to cover future files too
Access check order: owner → named users → owning group and named groups (masked, best match) → other. Named-user entries beat group entries
Preservation trap: `cp` drops ACLs unless you use `cp -a` or `--preserve=all`; `tar` needs `--acls`; rsync needs `-A`. Backups silently losing ACLs is common
Trade-off: ACLs are precise but invisible in `ls -l` beyond one `+`, and they are easy to drift. Prefer groups for coarse policy, ACLs for narrow exceptions

chapters.title: The Kernel's Decision Path: How a Check Actually Runs
points: Path resolution walks each component and requires x (MAY_EXEC) on every directory before the final component is even considered
For the target inode the kernel runs generic_permission(): if fsuid == owner UID use the user bits; else if the GID matches any group in the credential set use the group bits; else use other bits
This is first-match, not best-match — the kernel does not fall through to a more permissive class
If the DAC check fails, the kernel tries capabilities: CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE bypasses rwx entirely, CAP_DAC_READ_SEARCH bypasses read and directory search only
Capabilities are the modern, finer-grained alternative to setuid root: `setcap cap_net_bind_service=+ep ./server` lets a non-root binary bind port 80 without full root
After DAC, LSM hooks run — SELinux or AppArmor can still deny. "Permission denied" with correct-looking modes usually means an LSM or a nosuid/ro mount
Mount options override everything below them: `ro`, `noexec`, `nosuid`, `nodev` are enforced regardless of the inode's mode
Filesystems without Unix semantics (vfat, ntfs, many network mounts) fake permissions with mount options like `uid=`, `gid=`, `umask=`, `fmask=`, `dmask=` — chmod on them fails or is a no-op
NFS adds its own layers: `root_squash` maps remote root to nobody, and client-side attribute caching can make permission changes appear delayed
Debug order that resolves most cases: `namei -l /full/path` (checks every component), then `id`, then `stat`, then `mount | grep`, then `getfacl`, then `ausearch`/`dmesg` for AVC denials
`strace -e trace=openat,access ./prog` shows the exact failing syscall and errno — EACCES (permission) vs EPERM (privileged operation) vs ENOENT (a hidden traversal failure) tell different stories

chapters.title: Common Mistakes and Hard-Won Rules
points: `chmod -R 777` "to make it work": defeats the model entirely, and on web roots lets any local process rewrite your code. Diagnose with namei instead
`chmod -R 644 .` strips directory x and bricks the tree — always use `-R a+rX` for the recursive read case

Assuming permission falls through classes: `chmod 077` locks the owner out; `chmod 640` on a file whose owner is the service, when the service runs as a group member, still fails because owner-class matches first
Forgetting traversal: correct mode on the file, no x on a parent directory. The error mentions the file, the cause is upstream
Expecting setuid on a shell script to work — it is silently ignored. Reach for sudoers or capabilities
Changing umask and expecting existing files to update — umask is creation-time only
chmod'ing a file that has ACLs and destroying the mask without realizing it — verify with getfacl afterwards
Writable directory + non-writable file: a user can delete and replace a file they cannot edit. Protect the directory, not just the file
Sending files by tar/rsync/scp without preserving modes: `scp` drops setuid and can widen modes; `rsync -a` preserves standard bits but needs `-A -X` for ACLs and xattrs
Container UID mismatch: a bind-mounted host directory owned by UID 1000 is unwritable to a container process running as UID 999 — the names differ but only the numbers matter
Editors that rewrite rather than modify in place (write temp + rename) create the new file with your umask and lose the original mode and ACLs
Least privilege as the default: 644/755, tighten to 640/750 for service data, 600/700 for secrets, and treat every 777, world-writable directory, and unexpected setuid bit as a finding

chapters.title: Quick Reference and Recipes
points: Octal digits: 4=r, 2=w, 1=x. Special leading digit: 4=setuid, 2=setgid, 1=sticky
Symbolic cheatsheet: `u+x` add owner execute, `go-w` remove group/other write, `a=r` everyone read-only, `+t` sticky, `u+s` setuid, `g+s` setgid
Inspect: `ls -l`, `stat -c '%a %A %U %G %n'`, `namei -l path`, `getfacl`, `id`, `lsattr` (for chattr flags like +i immutable)
Standard secure defaults: files 644, directories 755, private files 600, private directories 700, secrets 400, shared project directories 2775 with umask 002
Shared team directory recipe: `mkdir /srv/proj && chgrp devs /srv/proj && chmod 2775 /srv/proj && setfacl -d -m g:devs:rwx /srv/proj`
Web root recipe: files 644, directories 755, owned by a deploy user, group-readable by the web server user — the web server should never own the code it serves
SSH recipe (sshd enforces this and refuses to work otherwise): ~/.ssh is 700, private keys 600, authorized_keys 600, and the home directory must not be group- or world-writable
Fix a broken tree: `find dir -type d -exec chmod 755 {} + ; find dir -type f -exec chmod 644 {} +`
Audit commands: `find / -xdev -perm -4000 -type f` (setuid), `find / -xdev -perm -0002 ! -type l` (world-writable), `find / -xdev -nouser -o -nogroup` (orphaned files)
Escalation ladder, least to most privilege: file permissions → groups → ACLs → file capabilities → sudo rules → setuid → root. Stop at the first rung that solves the problem

The three questions that solve nearly every permission bug: Who is the process (`id`)? What does the path require at every component (`namei -l`)? Is something above the filesystem overriding it (mount options, SELinux, container UID mapping)?
